chapter_theme: Songs at Chidambaram (சிதம்பரம், 2 of 5): the poet confesses his capture by women, their arts, their magic and their price, and once by the five senses and once by kin, wealth and learning, and asks for Murugan's feet, love and release; two songs ask to hold Murugan's form in mind even in the women's embrace. The praise centres on the hall (அம்பலம்) where Siva dances, Sivakami, and Murugan's place beside them.
structure_note: Songs on women (465 to 468, 473 to 475, 477, 478); the body as a bubble and the wish for release (469); the senses (464); a heap of self-abuse ending in a namo nama litany (470); a yogic song (471); a complaint that the Lord does not hear (472); and a song against kin, wealth and learning (476). 465 and 466 share a metre and opening, and 476 and 477 build each line on a repeated syllable or word.

464.reading: The poet calls himself a wretch who suffers the bewilderment, wavering and grief the bond of the five senses brings, with no steadiness or good quality, a fool and fickle, and asks that Murugan, recognising him as his old servant, give the lotus feet with golden anklets that Siva, wearing the serpent, the crescent, kurundu flowers, Brahma's skull and Ganga in his red hair, praises, sees with joy and worships. The praise shows the battlefield where jackals, dogs and red kites feast on heads, necks, tusks and bones, and the hall at Chidambaram where people come with austerity, japa and love.
464.nuance: The whole song runs in nasal-heavy syllables (தியங்குஞ்சஞ் சலந்துன்பங்), and the word divisions are often a guess. உன்றன் பழந்தொண்டு: the poet claims to be Murugan's servant of old. The feet asked for are those Siva himself worships (கும்பிடும் செம்பொன் சிலம்பு), so the son's feet are above the father's. The meaning of சிறுகூரா near the end is unclear.

465.reading: The poet describes women with breasts like elephant tusks, hair flashing like lightning, brows whirled like Indra's bow, carp eyes and practised touch, who destroy men with magic powder, and asks whether union with such deceivers is fitting. The praise shows Murugan taking a disguise in the forest to win and embrace Valli, sending the five syllables of Siva ahead in battle so the demon is struck down, and dwelling in the holy hall that the golden world praises daily.
465.nuance: மந்த்ர பொடிகொண்டு அழிக்கும் வஞ்சர்: the women's weapon is a charmed powder, a love-magic, which the praise answers with a holier spell: சிவம் அஞ்செழுத்தை முந்த விடுவோனே, the five syllables of Siva sent first against the asura. The line on Valli (ஒளிர்கொம்பினைச் சவுந்தரியவும் பலைக்கொணர்ந்து) does not divide clearly.

466.reading: The poet describes women with breasts like a rutting elephant's tusks under gem necklaces, with bangled hands, whose varied pleasing ways, smiles and coaxing he sees in excess, and asks not to be confused and deluded but, with doubt gone, to circle Murugan, praise him and receive the golden feet. The praise names Siva who wears the river, basil and moon and dances at Kailasa, and Vishnu who shot the arrow that shattered the heads and jewelled arms of the asura who tried to uproot that mountain, as Murugan's uncle, at the holy hall the gods worship daily.
466.nuance: The song is a twin of 465 in metre and opening (the breasts as an elephant's two tusks). The praise links two Ravana stories: the one who tried to pluck Kailasa in his hands (நகம் அங்கையில் பிடுங்கும் அசுரன்) is the one Rama's arrow destroyed. வலம்வந்து: the plea names the temple rite of circling.

467.reading: The poet describes women with moon faces, bow brows, carp eyes, cloud-dark hair, parrot speech and conch-white smiles, and lovemaking with them on the bed as Kama and Rati's pleasure, hair loosened, words faltering and eyes closing; he asks that even then Murugan grant him, alone as he is, the blissful moon faces and the beauty of the feet. The praise calls Sivakami the letter A, the life of all, who is also Hari and grows as a light in the poet's eye, and Murugan her son, whose vel destroyed the asura's army and before whom Brahma's head broke, the lord of Valli and Devayanai at the hall in southern Puliyur.
467.nuance: The plea seems not to ask to leave the bed but to be given Murugan's faces and feet there (மயல்கொண்டு அணைகீனும் ... அருள்வாயே), as 468 says outright. அகரம் திரு உயிர் பண்புற அரி என்பதுமாகி: Sivakami is the letter A and the life of letters, and also Hari, the Saiva teaching that Vishnu is a form of the Goddess. மறையன் தலை உடையும்படி may allude to Brahma's punishment.

468.reading: The poet describes women with moon-like earrings, Mandara-like breasts, champak-wreathed hair like cloud, carp eyes, crescent brows, kovai lips and conch necks, coaxing like heavenly dancers, and says that even if he sports with them on the bed in single desire, he will hold Murugan's twelve holy eyes and twelve strong arms. The praise shows Indra's world restored, sun and moon moving again and the Sura hosts dying, and Murugan teaching the mantra to Vishnu, Brahma, the sun, moon, Siva and Indra, with Valli, at the great hall of Chidambaram beside the Sivaganga tank that devotees call a pool of Tamil wisdom.
468.nuance: பஞ்சணை மீது குலாவினும் ... கொள்வேனே: unlike most songs, the plea does not renounce the women but vows to keep the Lord's form even in their embrace. மனு நூல் விளம்பிய: மனு is probably mantra, so this is Murugan as teacher of the gods. செந்தமிழ் ஞான தடாகம் ... சிவகங்கை: the temple tank is praised as a pool of Tamil wisdom.

469.reading: The poet calls the body a house of illusion, a nest that perishes like a bubble, a hut in which he daily seeks money and livelihood with his senses whirling and his mind astray, and asks not to suffer clinging to bamboo-shouldered women but to be given the single release that is complete in Vedic song, knowledge, silence, true wisdom and bliss. The praise names the vel that split the mountain, Valli's lover, the Vel of Senthil, the light where the Vedas, the seven notes and the five syllables sound, and the lord at the dance hall of the First Lord at Chidambaram.
469.nuance: காயம் மாய வீடு ... நந்து புற்புதம்: the body is a house of maya and a perishing bubble, an image the Naladiyar also uses. The goal is a single release (இன்ப முத்தி ஒன்று) in which Veda, knowledge, silence and bliss are all fulfilled. The song names both Senthil and Chidambaram.

470.reading: The poet heaps names on himself, man of vile qualities, ghoul-formed, dull and stupid, low in conduct, helpless, cruel, braggart, bound to the five elements, a waste born of a ruined womb, rotten, angry, shrouded by ill fortune, sinner, eunuch, drunkard who heeds no advice, and asks when Murugan will rule this dog of a servant. The praise names the serpent king of the netherworld, the Chola king of Manu's way and Indra praising the lord of Puliyur, and ends in a litany of 'namo nama' to the one who dances in the hall, gives the highest state by his sight, and burned the three cities.
470.nuance: The self-abuse is the longest yet, a run of rhymed names in -னை. The closing litany (சிவசிவ ஹரஹர தேவா நமோநம ... திரிபுரம் எரிசெய்த கோவே நமோநம) gives Murugan the acts of Siva, the dancer and burner of the three cities, or else turns to hail Siva himself; the text does not separate them. The serpent king (பாதாள லோகன்) is probably Patanjali of the Chidambaram legend; several of the abusive names are obscure.

471.reading: A yogic song: the poet asks whether, binding the fire at the root, driving it up to the crown, with bindu and sound crying out, mounting the white horse of mantra and attention, passing through the radiant hall, binding the bindu with the moon so it does not slip, burning the three cities to ash and striking down the tattvas, he will reach his Father's feet with sorrow burnt, eat wisdom, his body hard as diamond and golden, and praise Murugan. The praise calls Murugan the guru who spoke into the poet's ear the 'eight and two' he did not know, saying 'this is the lingam'; who, as a merchant, told the meaning to Siva who once sold bangles as a merchant in Sivakami's town; and who went to the forest as a merchant to win Valli, at the hall in Puliyur.
471.nuance: The plea is a map of the yogic ascent: fire (அங்கி) at the base, the cosmos above, bindu and nada, the moon, the burning of the three cities taken inwardly as the bonds, the tattvas falling, the body turned to diamond (குடில் வச்சிரங்களென). எட்டிரண்டு, 'eight and two', recurs six times; in Tamil numerals அ is eight and உ two, so the guru's teaching may be the letters of Om or Siva and Shakti, while elsewhere the phrase is the ten directions. செட்டி: Siva's bangle-selling and Murugan's courting of Valli are both played as merchant disguises.

472.reading: The poet says that, judging it evil to trust deceitful talebearers with poisoned minds, he sought Murugan's feet with love and cried 'our father, refuge', and asks whether this has not reached his ear, or whether his eyes are on his women; no one can defy his word, the burden is his, and the poet has no other helper, so let him come and appear as he did for the gods. The praise shows Murugan knocking Brahma on the head, embracing Valli and shaking the mountains and seas, the lord of Siva who dances in the hall at Puliyur.
472.nuance: உன்செவிக் கேறலைகொல் பெண்கள்மெற் பார்வையைகொல்: the poet chides the Lord, asking whether he is deaf or too busy looking at his wives, an intimacy of complaint. உன்றனக்கே பரமும்: the burden of saving him belongs to the Lord. The knock on Brahma's head (கஞ்சனைத் தாவி முடி முன்பு குட்டே) recalls the Om story without naming Om.

473.reading: A short song: the poet asks not to waver in mind over women with breasts like red pots until his body wastes, but to be given grace so that he melts in love. The praise names Murugan who holds the banner in his red hand, the poet who knows fine words, the son of Uma, growing in the hall.
473.nuance: செஞ்சொல்தெரி புலவோனே: Murugan is himself the poet who discerns fine speech.

474.reading: The poet runs through a woman's beauty, cloud hair, bow brows, carp-arrow eyes, moon forehead, areca neck, bamboo arms, mountain breasts, lotus hands, plantain thighs, drum waist and fine silk, and calls such women, dancing like peacocks, without good qualities; he asks whether he must be caught in their net and perish, and asks for Murugan's love. The praise names Sivai, the self-born, the beauty of all worlds, as his mother, the fiery vel thrown at the asura army, Vishnu who killed Ravana and holds the fourteen worlds as his uncle, and Devayanai and Valli, at Chidambaram.
474.nuance: The beauty is catalogued only to be set against இயல் குணமிலாத வியன் செயலார், women of display with no good nature. பொருள் சங்க மாதர் may mean women joined for money, but the division is unsure.

475.reading: The poet describes lovemaking in detail, hair loosening, garlands crushed, eyes troubled, sandal paste washed by sweat, lips tasted like jackfruit segments and voices cooing like doves and peacocks, and asks whether he, a dog, must be ruined and fall with his body wasting. The praise shows the battle in drum syllables, Sura's crown smashed and the seven seas dried by the vel, Murugan dancing, and Chidambaram of mango groves, cuckoos, plantain and cane, where Sivakami and the hunter girl bow to him.
475.nuance: The plea is only a question at the end of the scene (நாயென அழிந்து விழுந்து உடல் மங்குவேனோ): the ruin is the body's fading.

476.reading: The poet asks that, free of the trouble called father, mother, house, stored gold and silver, the rich who seek them, learning and kin, he sing Murugan as best he can, and asks whether this complete fool's withering will not end while his heart fails to know him as the freed one, the swift one, the Lord, Valli's beloved. The praise names Murugan the child born from the eye of the dancer of Thillai, holding the red vel of power, worn by devotees who speak the truth, and embracing Devayanai, with green vanni, lilies and vetchi on his head and the green peacock.
476.nuance: கல்வி stands in the list of bonds with gold, silver and kin: learning too is a trouble (அல்லல்) to be shed before one can sing. Each line pair turns on repeated syllables (அத்தன், அத்தை, அத்து; முத்தன், முத்தன், முட்டன்), so several words (அத்து, பட்டன், முத்தன்) can be read more than one way.

477.reading: The poet speaks of women who show dark hair, bow brows, eyes like killing lilies, jasmine smiles and creeper waists, who show delusion and then show poverty, and asks whether Murugan, who can show the path that does not end at the burning ground, show good understanding and slowly wither karma, should let him suffer. The praise names Murugan the young lord of Thillai, which shows clarity, the ancient Veda and rich speech, Valli of the millet field, the one who shows grace and the path of learning, and the good lord of devotees who praise his feet.
477.nuance: The verb காட்டு, to show, runs through every line: the women show their charms and then poverty (நல்குரவு காட்டும்), the Lord shows the path past the cremation ground (இடுகாட்டின் எல்லை நடவாத வழி), and Thillai shows wisdom. The play joins காட்டு with இடுகாடு, the burning ground.

478.reading: The poet runs through a woman's beauty from smile to anklets, her walk swaying in silk, and calls such women plunderers of gold like skilled thieves, and asks whether infatuation with them is fitting. The praise names Murugan who, so that troubling deeds and the gunas flee, holds the poet's heart as his own and rules it, who taught the seed of wisdom to delight his father, Valli whom the poet calls his own mother, the vel, and the lord who rejoices at the tower of Thillai with Devayanai, sung in clear Tamil.
478.nuance: பொற் சூறை கொண்டார்கள்: the women plunder gold like raiders. எந்தாதை மகிழ ... ஞானவித்து ஓது: Murugan teaching his father the seed of wisdom, the Om story without the word. என்னுடைய தாய்: Valli is called the poet's mother.

links.note: Both see the body as a bubble that forms and bursts; the Naladiyar praises the firm who resolve from this to end their wandering, and 469 asks from it for the one release complete in wisdom, silence and bliss.
The Kural makes the letter A first of letters as the Lord is first of the world; 467 takes the letter itself as a name of the Goddess, calling Sivakami the அகரம் and the life of all.

Both ask not to leave the bed but to hold the Lord there: 468 vows to keep the twelve eyes and twelve arms even while sporting with women, and 467 asks for the moon faces and feet in the same embrace.
Both make poverty the end of the courtesan's love: the Naladiyar's flood ends when the income ends, and 477's women first show delusion and then show poverty.

The song calls the poet a wretch suffering the bond of the five senses (ஐந்திந்த்ரிய பந்தம் தரும் துன்பம் படும் ஏழை), with no steadiness, fickle (சலன்). Tirumular confesses the same failure in his own voice: வெல்லகில்லேன் புலன் ஐந்துடன் தன்னையும், he is like a horse that bolts. Both are first-person admissions, not instructions; the song adds the remedy Tirumular leaves unsaid, that the Lord recognise him as his old servant (உன்றன் பழந்தொண்டு).

The song's women destroy men with a charmed powder (மந்த்ர பொடிகொண்டு அழிக்கும் வஞ்சர்), and the praise answers with Murugan who sends Siva's five syllables first into battle (சிவம் அஞ்செழுத்தை முந்த விடுவோனே). Tirumular says that once the truth of the five letters is known there is no deceit (வஞ்சகம் இல்லை) and no ruin to the house. Together they set the five syllables against வஞ்சம, the holy spell against the deceivers' spell.

The song asks that, doubt cast off and understanding (விடுசங்கையற்று உணர்ந்து), the poet circle Murugan, praise him and receive his golden feet. The Kural says that for those who have left doubt and become clear (ஐயத்தின் நீங்கித் தெளிந்தார்க்கு) the sky is nearer than the earth. The song makes the Kural's step a plea within worship: the shedding of doubt is what lets the circling and the praise reach the feet.

After its heap of self-abuse the song hails the Lord as the one who became the highest state by being seen (தெரிசன பரகதி யானாய் நமோநம). Tirumular makes clarity itself consist in seeing the guru's holy form (தெளிவு குருவின் திருமேனி காண்டல்). The pairing shows the litany's title as the Saiva teaching that the sight of the Lord or guru is itself the gift; the reading of தெரிசன பரகதி as 'the goal given by sight' is the one this depends on.

The song calls Murugan the guru who spoke into an ear that did not know the eight and two (எட்டிரண்டும் அறியாத என்செவியில்) and said 'this is the lingam'. Tirumular's verse turns on the same phrase and almost the same words: எட்டும் இரண்டும் அறியாத ஏழையர் miss that the eight and two are the step of the Siddhanta path. The song places itself among Tirumular's ignorant and names the guru's whispered teaching as what cured it; what the eight and two stand for is unsettled in both.

The song turns from deceitful talebearers with poisoned minds to the Lord and says, the burden is yours, for who is my helper (உன்றனக்கே பரமும் என்றனக்கு ஆர் துணைவர்). Tirumular runs துணை four times: make Nandi your close support (உறுதுணை), and he stands as support. Both make the Lord the only துணை; the song speaks it as a complaint that the Lord has not yet come.

Tirumular commands the hearer to melt his own love (என் அன்புருக்கி ... முன் அன்புருக்கி) before seeking the Lord, after which the Lord's love answers. The short song, wavering over women, cannot do this itself and asks for it as grace: அன்புருக அருள்வாயே. The pairing shows the melting of love that Tirumular sets as the devotee's work turned into the Lord's gift.

The song catalogues a woman's beauty from hair to waist and then calls such women without good nature (இயல் குணமிலாத), a net in which he will perish. Tirumular says the ripe etti fruit cannot be eaten however good its leaves and clusters, so the heart must hold back from women who smile and display their breasts (முலைநலம் கொண்டு முறுவல் செய்வார்). Both set the beauty on show against what lies under it.

The song tastes the woman's lips like jackfruit segments (பலாசுளையின் சுவை கண்டு இதழ் உண்டு) and ends by asking whether he must fall like a dog with his body wasting. The Kural's lover finds the water at his beloved's teeth like milk mixed with honey (பாலொடு தேன் கலந்தற்றே). The same image of the mouth's sweetness is joy in the Kural's love and the prelude to ruin in the song.

The song lists learning (கல்வி) with father, mother, house, gold, silver and kin as a trouble (அல்லல்) to be shed before he can sing the Lord. The Kural calls learning the one imperishable wealth (கேடில் விழுச்செல்வம் கல்வி), other things not wealth. The conflict holds on the reading that the song counts learning itself as a bond; if அத்து பண்ணு கல்வி means only learning pursued for gain, it narrows to a qualification.

The song says the women, after their show of beauty, plunder gold like skilled raiders (வல்லவர்கள் போல பொற்சூறை கொண்டார்கள்) and asks whether infatuation with them is fitting. The Naladiyar's woman licks like a wild cow, takes the wealth from the man's hands (அவர்கைப் பொருள்கொண்டு) and turns away, and those who thought her love theirs are laughed at. Both name the taking of wealth as the purpose behind the display.

source_issues: Song 474: one corrupt character in கமுக க்஡ணவர் (line 4), probably க்ரீவர், 'areca-like neck', with ஡ண for ரீ.
Song 478: unflagged garble வழ்ழைதொடை (line 9), probably வாழைத்தொடை; முன்னல்கமு (line 6) is also doubtful.
Song 464: சிறுகூரா (line 21) is unclear and may be corrupt.
